summary: God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, whom he loves, as a burnt offering in Moriah. Abraham binds Isaac and takes the knife, but an angel stops him; a ram is offered instead, blessing is restated, and a final family notice names Rebekah among Nahor’s descendants.
whyItMatters: The promised son’s life is put in danger within the test, while the narrative ends by explicitly prohibiting harm to him and providing a substitute. Its disturbing command cannot be treated as a general model for violence toward children.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The journey from Beersheba toward a mountain in Moriah and the return to Beersheba.
context.literaryForm: Test and near-sacrifice narrative followed by reiterated blessing and a short kinship list.

before.text: Sarah has borne Isaac, while Hagar and Ishmael have been sent away and rescued. Isaac’s survival now becomes the issue in a new test of Abraham.

here.text: Follow what Abraham is commanded, what he actually does to Isaac, the angel’s interruption, and the ram offered instead.

after.text: Sarah dies in Canaan, and Abraham negotiates and pays for a burial place for her.

outline.heading: The test and journey
outline.note: God commands Isaac’s offering; Abraham prepares and travels to the place.

outline.heading: Isaac asks about the lamb
outline.note: Father and son carry the materials together, and Isaac questions the missing animal.

outline.heading: Binding and angelic intervention
outline.note: Abraham binds Isaac and raises the knife; an angel orders him not to touch the boy.

outline.heading: Ram and place name
outline.note: A ram is offered instead of Isaac, and Abraham names the place for provision.

outline.heading: Blessing repeated and return
outline.note: The angel restates offspring and worldwide blessing; Abraham returns to Beersheba.

outline.heading: Nahor’s descendants
outline.note: A family notice introduces Rebekah and other relatives.

keyVerses.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
keyVerses.why: The test begins with an explicit command involving the loved promised son.

keyVerses.text: He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.”
keyVerses.why: The angel’s prohibition stops violence against Isaac before the ram appears.

keyVerses.text: Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering instead of his son.
keyVerses.why: The text says the ram is offered instead of the son.

questions.question: Does the chapter command anyone today to harm a child?
questions.answer: The narrative opens by calling this a test of Abraham, then reports a command concerning Isaac in that specific story. An angel stops Abraham and says not to lay a hand on the boy; the passage supplies no general authorization for harming children.

questions.question: How close does Abraham come to killing Isaac?
questions.answer: He builds the altar, binds Isaac, lays him on the wood, and takes the knife to kill him. The angel interrupts before a blow is struck, and a ram is used for the offering instead.

questions.question: Why does Abraham call the place “Yahweh Will Provide”?
questions.answer: After Isaac asks where the lamb is, Abraham says God will provide, and he later finds a ram caught in a thicket. The place name remembers that substitute within this episode.

questions.question: Does “your only son” mean Ishmael never existed?
questions.answer: No. Earlier chapters name Ishmael as Abraham’s son and describe God’s promise to him. “Only son” is the wording of this test scene about Isaac; it should not be used to erase Ishmael from the book’s own family story.

questions.question: What does Isaac say or do during the journey?
questions.answer: He carries the wood and asks where the lamb for the offering is; Abraham answers that God will provide. The narrative does not record Isaac agreeing to be bound, nor does it specify his age here.

questions.question: What does the angel say the test has shown?
questions.answer: The angel says Abraham fears God because he has not withheld Isaac, and then prohibits harm. A second angelic speech repeats promises of many offspring and blessing for nations in connection with Abraham’s obedience.

questions.question: How should the absence of Isaac in the return sentence be read?
questions.answer: Verse 19 says Abraham returns to the young men and they go to Beersheba; it does not separately name Isaac in that sentence. The text does not narrate Isaac’s death, and the interruption explicitly saved him, so absence from a list is not evidence he was killed.

questions.question: Why end with Nahor’s family list?
questions.answer: It names children in Abraham’s brother’s household and specifically identifies Bethuel as Rebekah’s father. That notice prepares the later account of finding a wife for Isaac without becoming part of the mountain test itself.

glossary.def: The sacrifice God commands Abraham to make, ultimately performed with the ram rather than Isaac.
The named region of the mountain to which Abraham travels for the test.
The tangled growth where the substitute ram is caught by its horns.
